extracted.intended_audience: readers skeptical of mainstream media and climate science orthodoxy (Iowa Climate Science Education audience)
extracted.subtask_short: opinion blog post on media scandal
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/analysis blog entry criticizing Der Spiegel's fabrication scandal and using it to argue broader failings in German/Western mainstream journalism, especially on climate issues. Aimed at readers skeptical of mainstream media and climate-policy consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / No fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must be factually true; fabrication (inventing stories or details) is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece centers on Claas Relotius 'fabricating stories' over years (e.g., Fergus Falls), showing how invented anecdotes and claims destroyed credibility. Example/anti-pattern: journalist inventing characters or incidents to 'smear' subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial fact‑checking and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and newsroom processes must catch falsehoods and verify reporting before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article asks 'How could this have gotten by Spiegel editors?' and argues editorial failure allowed fabrications to persist. Anti-pattern: editors publishing pieces that merely 'appeal to them' without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutionalized bias / neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should avoid long‑running one-sided or activist reporting and institutionalized prejudices (e.g., anti‑Americanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author claims Relotius reflected 'Spiegel’s institutionalized overzealous anti‑Americanism' and that the problem is not an isolated renegade but an ingrained sentiment. Evaluators should look for patterns across stories, not treat incidents as anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotyping and smear
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not depict groups using derogatory clichés or aim to viciously smear communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relotius is accused of inventing stories to portray 'rural American Trump voters as contemptible, small‑minded, gun‑toting, right‑wing religious rednecks.' Anti-pattern: relying on caricatures and cliche‑filled depictions instead of nuanced reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source verification and use of primary/local sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and anecdotes must be verifiable by contacting primary/local sources and checking publicly available information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Medium writers found 'so many lies' in the Fergus Falls piece that 'a child could figure out in a Google search.' Anti-pattern: failing to contact local residents or primary documents that would refute invented claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cherry‑picking/selective facts to fit a narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should not rely solely on carefully selected facts that tailor a preconceived narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited example: Die Zeit’s feature allegedly 'relied solely on carefully selected “facts” to tailor a narrative' that climate skepticism was orchestrated. Evaluators should check whether reporting omits relevant counterevidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and pluralism — provide forum to dissenting views
rubrics_metrics.description: Media should allow reasoned dissenting or skeptical perspectives rather than declaring open‑season on certain viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticizes the BBC and LA Times for 'declared not to provide a forum to climate deniers,' framing that as censorship. Criterion: whether outlets give fair hearing to non‑mainstream voices (subject to accuracy standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate labeling of critics vs. deniers
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators should accurately characterize skeptics' positions and not conflate skepticism with denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues skeptics 'don’t deny climate change', 'agree that man has an impact' but differ on magnitude/urgency. Anti-pattern: dismissing skeptics as 'deniers' without precise distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, accountability, and proportional response
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets must transparently address scandals, accept accountability, and avoid minimizing systemic problems as isolated incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiegel's strategy 'to make Relotius look as if he was just an isolated renegade' is criticized; the piece urges acknowledging broader institutional issues rather than scapegoating one reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from PR/industry influence and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative claims about movements or campaigns should be scrutinized for dependence on PR or industry narratives and conflicts of interest disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Die Zeit's feature accusing industry‑funded PR of manufacturing climate denial is cited as an example where journalists may accept an orchestration thesis without broader evidence. Evaluators should examine sources and motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid one‑sided 'hit pieces' — ensure proportionality and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Features and exposés should avoid becoming 'hit pieces' that rely on a single thesis and omit context or rebuttal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article labels some reporting as 'one‑sided hit piece' and 'half‑truth journalism.' Metric: whether the piece presents counterarguments, diverse sources, and proportional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and long‑term reputational risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A single scandal's effect on an outlet's credibility should be assessed in light of past practices and the scope of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asserts 'It’s doubtful Spiegel ... will ever recover its credibility' given fabrications 'went on for years and involved dozens of major stories.' Evaluators should weigh historical patterns when judging reputational damage.
